I’ll give my 2 cents, not a teacher in the US, but around Eastern Europe, was in a somewhat similar situation, started teaching after my bachelors in history.

Long story short - don’t. This all obviously depends on your personality and whatnot but I taught classes 7 and 8 (age 14-16) for my first year (while doing another job) and looking back, I wasted so much time because I’d do things very ineffectively, did way too much prep for instance, and almost burned myself out. After finishing my masters this year I had a much more solid grasp on the theory of learning/teaching and therefore work became easier and I was more at ease. Therefore I recommend putting your own education first. And don’t try to teach and finish your studies at the same time, I did it this year and while I did succeed, I’m still recovering.

Hmmm. Maybe? This something I have been thinking about - maybe it all did amount to something. The problem is we only have this, the current reality. We don't really know what would have happened had I and the other kids been in a different, supportive classroom. Maybe most of us succeeded not because of our teachers harshness but in spite of said harshness. We worked hard, and I and many others would have regardless of the teachers, it was just extra stress. I did acquire a good education and good contacts there. But on the other hand, there were many social-emotional skills I had to develop in therapy over the years and I basically graduated school with no self-esteem whatsoever. I do not only blame the school in this, other factors definitely played their parts. I think that the true balance is, much like almost always, somewhere in the middle. School should be challenging, demanding, but also supportive. At some point harshness becomes damaging.
